cards.key_problem: TCP-based SSL tunnels give poor, jittery VoIP, video and heavy-graphics performance over the internet and cannot give each user a fixed IP, which VoIP systems, NAC, web proxies and DoT rules need.
key_outcomes: Two endpoints: TLS 1.2 on TCP 443 for authentication, device checks and key distribution; Noise protocol on UDP 443 for the data tunnel

Cryptography: ChaCha20-Poly1305, Curve25519 ECDH, BLAKE2s, SipHash24, HKDF; NoiseIK one-round-trip handshake; rekey every 120 s; perfect forward secrecy, identity hiding, replay and KCI resistance; IP-binding cookies against DoS; ~4,000 lines of kernel code; references the WireGuard paper
Optional 256-bit pre-shared symmetric key (e.g. delivered via MDM) for post-quantum resistance; encryption workflow in six steps
Benchmarks: 1,011 Mbps vs 825-881 Mbps IPsec and 258 Mbps OpenVPN; 0.403 ms latency vs 0.51-0.52 ms and 1.54 ms

Unique static virtual IP per user every login, NAT'ed on the gateway or routed internally; DNS proxy with redirect list; step-by-step packet flows (addresses and MACs) for NAT, masquerade and route modes
Use cases: VoIP from PC or phone, mobile apps, VoIP/Teams/WebEx over VDI, backups, SCCM, always-on domain traffic, per-user IP for NAC/proxies, UDP multicast trading apps; ships in HySecure 5.4
cards.brief: The deepest document in the library on how HySecure's Turbo tunnel works. cards.title: WireGuard: Next Generation Kernel Network Tunnel - Jason A. Donenfeld (Third-Party Protocol Paper, NDSS 2017; Draft Revision June 2020)
cards.key_problem: IPsec and OpenVPN are complex, large and hard to audit; WireGuard proposes a small, fast, secure layer-3 tunnel.
key_outcomes: Design: layer-3 kernel virtual interface; 'cryptokey routing' binding peer public keys to allowed IPs; roaming endpoints

Protocol: 1-RTT NoiseIK handshake, Curve25519 static keys (OpenSSH style), ChaCha20-Poly1305 transport over UDP, optional pre-shared symmetric key, encrypted and authenticated cookie MACs against DoS, timer state machine, 'silence is a virtue' (no response to unauthenticated packets)
Implementation in under 4,000 lines of Linux code; performance comparisons with IPsec and OpenVPN
Static link wireguard.com/papers/wireguard.pdf; draft revision dated 1 June 2020; version in NDSS 2017 proceedings
cards.brief: The original WireGuard protocol paper by its author, covering cryptokey routing, send/receive flow, the Noise-based handshake and cryptography, cookie DoS mitigation, the timer state machine, Linux kernel implementation and performance. Accops keeps it in the HySecure/Turbo folder because HySecure Turbo is built on WireGuard's design; the Accops Turbo deck cites it as its reference.
cards.use_for: Technical assurance for a network architect or CISO asking whether the Turbo tunnel's cryptography is sound - send the public link alongside the Accops Turbo Architecture v2 deck. Not Accops collateral.
cards.stale_risk: Draft revision of June 2020 of a 2017 paper; the protocol is stable, but the published version on wireguard.com may be newer.
cards.needs_human: Third-party paper - share the public link rather than the SharePoint copy. Reps should say 'Turbo is based on the WireGuard design', not that Accops wrote or certified it.
cards.third_party_copyright: Copyright 2015-2020 Jason A. Donenfeld. Publicly available paper.

cards.title: Formal Verification of the WireGuard Protocol - Donenfeld and Milner (Oxford), Tamarin Prover Proofs (Third-Party Paper, June 2018)
cards.key_problem: Security claims for a VPN handshake need independent, machine-checked proof.
key_outcomes: Enumerates the security properties of WireGuard's NoiseIK-based key exchange and verifies them in the Tamarin prover
Properties covered include key secrecy, forward secrecy, mutual authentication, key-compromise impersonation resistance, replay resistance and a limited form of identity hiding
Draft revision dated 7 June 2018; static link wireguard.com/papers/wireguard-formal-verification.pdf
cards.brief: An academic paper by WireGuard's author and an Oxford University researcher that models the WireGuard key exchange and proves its security properties with the Tamarin symbolic verification tool, including the caveats on identity hiding. Filed with the Accops HySecure Turbo material as third-party evidence for the protocol Turbo is based on.
cards.use_for: Answering 'has the tunnel protocol been formally verified?' in a security review or RFP - cite with the public link, alongside the Turbo Architecture v2 deck.

cards.needs_human: Third-party paper - share the public link. It verifies WireGuard, not Accops' Turbo implementation.
cards.third_party_copyright: Copyright 2017 Jason A. Donenfeld & Kevin Milner. Publicly available paper.

cards.key_problem: Independent review of the parts of WireGuard not covered by formal proofs - reconnection, session management and timers.
key_outcomes: Partial security audit by three MIT students, focused on unverified reconnection and session-management code, using network fuzzing with artificial latency and packet loss
Found WireGuard 'generally functions as it should'; no critical bugs; robust under 80% packet loss
Found a timer-system implementation bug and a double-handshake scenario; recommended rounding the handshake-retransmission timer up and simplifying the send-keepalive timer
cards.brief: A 2018 MIT 6.857 (Computer and Network Security) final project that audits WireGuard's session and timer logic by fuzzing across cloud nodes, reports good behaviour under adverse networks and two implementation issues, and recommends fixes. cards.use_for: Supporting evidence in a security questionnaire about the tunnel protocol behind Turbo. Lower weight than the formal proofs - it is a student project.

cards.title: A Mechanised Cryptographic Proof of the WireGuard VPN Protocol - Lipp, Blanchet, Bhargavan (Inria Research Report RR-9269, 2019, CryptoVerif)
cards.key_problem: Symbolic proofs alone do not give computational cryptographic guarantees for the full protocol including transport data.
key_outcomes: First mechanised computational proof of the whole WireGuard protocol, including transport data messages, using the CryptoVerif proof assistant in an ACCE-style model
Proves correctness, message secrecy, forward secrecy, mutual authentication, session uniqueness and resistance to key-compromise impersonation, identity mis-binding and replay
Discusses the strength of WireGuard's identity hiding; 49-page Inria report (April 2019, revised June 2019), HAL id hal-02100345v2

cards.use_for: The strongest third-party assurance for the Turbo tunnel's cryptography in a security review; cite with the public HAL link and the Turbo Architecture v2 deck.
